summary: France is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorisation being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90, applied for via the official France-Visas portal.

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since 11 June 2024.

For stays over 90 days: work, family and other long-stay purposes. Many long-stay visas act as residence permits (VLS-TS) and must be validated online within 3 months of arrival. Confirm the fee for your category on France-Visas.
Reduced fee for students going through the Études en France / Campus France procedure; €99 otherwise. Requires proof of enrolment, funds and accommodation. Confirm the current fee on France-Visas.
For highly skilled employees, investors, researchers, artists and start-up founders; leads to a multi-year residence permit of up to 4 years. Confirm your category's conditions on France-Visas.
Requires a work authorisation obtained by the employer in France before the visa application.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: France scales the means requirement by accommodation: roughly €65 per day with prepaid accommodation, €120 per day without proof of accommodation, and about €32.50 per day with a validated attestation d'accueil (host certificate). Confirm current figures on France-Visas.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border — there is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorisation System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere, including bakeries and taxis. Some cafés apply a small card minimum, so a little cash is handy.

safety.text: France is a safe destination overall. The main risks for visitors are pickpocketing on the Paris metro and around major sights, common tourist scams, and occasional demonstrations or transport strikes.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — France Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–June and September–October offer mild weather and thinner crowds; July–August is peak season, and many Paris businesses close in August while the coast fills up.

tips.text: Pickpocketing and distraction scams (petitions, gold rings, friendship bracelets) are common on the Paris metro and around major sights — keep valuables zipped away.
Transport strikes (grèves) periodically disrupt trains, the metro and flights — check SNCF and airport status before travel days and build in slack.
The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just France — days spent in Spain or Italy count against the same allowance.
Apply for ETIAS only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site once it becomes mandatory — unofficial sites charge inflated fees.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for France?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit France and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorisation (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a France Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11, applied for via the official France-Visas portal. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter France?
faq.answer: ETIAS is being phased in for visa-exempt travellers. During the transition period travellers without ETIAS are still admitted; once fully mandatory, the €20 online authorisation will be required before boarding. Check the official EU website for the current status.

faq.question: How do I stay in France longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: You need a national long-stay visa (Type D), applied for via France-Visas before travel — typically around €99 (€50 for Campus France students). Many long-stay visas (VLS-TS) double as residence permits and must be validated online within 3 months of arrival.

faq.question: Is travel insurance mandatory for France?
faq.answer: It is mandatory for Schengen visa applicants: medical cover of at least €30,000 valid throughout the Schengen Area. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to present insurance, though it is strongly recommended.
